deep.reconstruction:
Context: this folio continues Riemann's draft remarks for the public disputation accompanying his doctoral promotion at Göttingen, December 1851. The reference on the previous page to Cauchy's Paris Academy session of 31 March 'dieses Jahrs' fixes the year as 1851. There he defends the definition from his dissertation (Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse): w is a function of z = x+iy when the value of dw/dz does not depend on the differential dz.

He lists two opposing views. The first attributes this property to complex functions but derives it from a supposedly proven lemma: the derivative of a function of a+b with respect to a equals its derivative with respect to b. The second is Cauchy's 1851 view, in which any complex quantity varying with x+iy counts as a function of x+iy.

The previous page ends with Riemann starting to examine that lemma. While a, b and the function are real, he says, it follows immediately from the concept of a derivative: 'Denn von einem Differentialquotienten kann man nur'. This page completes the sentence:

'... reden, wenn sich das Verhältniß des Zuwachses von a+b zu dem entsprechenden Zuwachse der Function einer festen Grenze nähert, sobald man diesen Zuwachs unendlich klein werden läßt. Es ist aber dabei offenbar einerlei, ob man diesen Zuwachs als einen Zuwachs von a, oder als einen Zuwachs von b betrachtet.'

In modern terms, let F(a,b) = f(a+b) with f differentiable. Then:
- ∂F/∂a = lim_{h→0} [f(a+h+b) − f(a+b)]/h = f'(a+b).
- ∂F/∂b = lim_{h→0} [f(a+b+h) − f(a+b)]/h = f'(a+b).
- Hence ∂F/∂a = ∂F/∂b.

The point is that a derivative of f at s = a+b is defined through increments of s only. Whether the increment h comes from a or from b is irrelevant, so the equality is trivial in the real case.

Implicit continuation (my inference, not on this page): the argument transfers to complex arguments a = x, b = iy only if f already has a derivative in s = x+iy that is independent of the direction of the increment. That is precisely Riemann's defining property. Applied to f(x+iy), the lemma gives ∂f/∂(iy) = ∂f/∂x, i.e. ∂f/∂y = i ∂f/∂x, which is the Cauchy–Riemann equations. So the 'previously proven lemma' presupposes what it is meant to justify. This is why Riemann insists the property belongs in the definition.

The remainder of the page carries no writing; the faint text is bleed-through from the other side of the sheet.
errors: Riemann writes the ratio as 'increment of a+b to the corresponding increment of the function'. This is the reciprocal of the difference quotient dw/dz. As a statement about the existence of a limit it is harmless where f' ≠ 0, but strictly it is inverted (and fails when f' = 0). This is a slip of phrasing rather than of mathematics.
No other errors. The argument is correct for real a, b, f.

results.what: For f(a+b) the partial derivatives with respect to a and with respect to b coincide, because the derivative depends only on the increment of the sum. This holds trivially in the real case, and in the complex case only if the derivative is direction-independent.
results.modern_name: Chain rule for f(a+b); in the complex setting it amounts to the Cauchy–Riemann equations / complex differentiability
results.usually_credited_to: Routine calculus; the definition of complex differentiability as direction-independence of dw/dz is Riemann 1851 (dissertation), with Cauchy and d'Alembert/Euler as antecedents

results.what: Methodological critique: the property dw/dz independent of dz must be part of the definition of a complex function and cannot be derived from the real-variable lemma. Placed in the context of Cauchy's 31 March 1851 Academy remarks on Puiseux.

deep.surprise_reason: This is part of Riemann's draft for his 1851 doctoral disputation, defending the well-known definition from his dissertation. The mathematics is elementary and the definition is famously his. The only mildly interesting detail is the explicit polemical context (Cauchy's 1851 remarks on Puiseux), which is of historical rather than mathematical note.

checkable.asserts: d/da f(a+b) = d/db f(a+b) for differentiable f
For a complex-differentiable function of x+iy, dw/dy = i dw/dx (Cauchy–Riemann), i.e. the a/b lemma with b=iy
Returns False: conj(z) = x-iy, a function of x and y in Cauchy's broad sense, violates the lemma. This shows the lemma presupposes Riemann's definition.

transcription_corrections: First word: 'werden[?]' should read 'reden', completing 'kann man nur reden, wenn...'.
'von $a+b$[?]' is correct as 'von a+b'; the uncertainty mark can be removed.
The rest of the page is blank apart from show-through of the reverse side, so nothing further needs transcribing.
